challenges.description:
As Staff Engineer at Viterbit, I work across the product platform and the engineering system that supports its development and delivery. My role combines hands-on software development, technical leadership, architecture, developer experience and engineering quality. I build platform functionality using AI agents, review and harden the generated code, establish the necessary quality and architectural guardrails, and help define the development and delivery pipelines that make agent-assisted development reliable and maintainable.

I am responsible for building and integrating viterbit-ui, Viterbit’s shared design system for Symfony applications. The library provides more than 170 reusable Symfony Twig Components, built with Tailwind CSS 4, semantic theming, dark-mode support, Symfony UX, Stimulus controllers and AssetMapper. I work on the component APIs, interaction patterns, accessibility, server-side rendering and integration into the main web application, ensuring that the system remains consistent and usable across different product areas.

I also build and maintain vdev, Viterbit’s development CLI. It manages local web-app workspaces using Git worktrees, Docker Compose stacks, shared Traefik routing, local HTTPS, data synchronisation, workers and maintenance commands. It also supports complete remote workspaces where the application, workers and supporting data services run on shared infrastructure. This work focuses on reducing the friction of creating, operating and debugging development environments, while providing predictable workflows and agent-friendly output for automated tooling.

Alongside these platform initiatives, I contribute directly to web-app, a large Symfony and MongoDB product codebase. My work spans recruitment campaigns and career-site flows, Talent Community automation, candidate lifecycle features, AI-assisted recruitment, interviews and calendar workflows, as well as the APIs and platform services behind them. I work across application, domain, infrastructure and integration layers, translating product requirements into maintainable implementations while preserving architectural boundaries and tenant isolation.

A significant part of my role is improving engineering quality across the system. This includes reviewing pull requests and AI-generated changes, enforcing architectural conventions, improving CI workflows, investigating performance issues such as MongoDB indexes used by reporting, and addressing security concerns such as SVG upload vulnerabilities and clickjacking protections. I remain hands-on while helping the team establish development practices that allow a fast-moving product organisation to ship safely and consistently.

In charge of a team of five engineers, responsible for the planning, development, and as far as possible, the success of one of the latest projects of the company, Leaploot , a webapp focused on incentive marketing. We use Laravel 12 and PHP 8.4. Although this time we do not employ Domain-Driven Design (DDD), which does not align well with Laravel, we strive to maintain focus on SOLID principles, best practices, and clean code.

I was promoted to Head of Technology at Scalefast, taking responsibility for the development of three strategic areas of the next-generation e-commerce platform: the Order Management System (OMS), Fulfillment and logistics, and Core/Platform.

OMS covered the order lifecycle, while Fulfillment covered warehouse operations, logistics, delivery, and returns. Core/Platform provided the foundation, shared infrastructure, and Domain-Driven Design framework used by the other domain contexts. The platform was being designed to replace a large V4 monolith with a service-oriented V5 architecture.

I coordinated three engineering squads with approximately 20 people in total. Each squad had a Team Lead and four or five developers, with different levels of experience ranging from senior and staff engineers to junior developers. My responsibilities included technical coordination across teams, architecture definition, mentoring Team Leads and engineers, resolving cross-context design issues, supporting technical decision-making and working with Product Managers on roadmap definition, priorities and sequencing.

The main architectural initiative was the simplification of the DDD framework used across the platform. We moved away from a Laravel-centred foundation and developed a lighter in-house framework based on Slim 4, Doctrine and robust, well-established components from the PHP ecosystem. The platform was primarily built with PHP 8.2, with OpenSwoole used for selected runtime workloads. Slim 4 acted as the API glue, while the architecture remained deliberately focused on clear boundaries and minimal framework coupling.

The foundation established common patterns for PSR-compliant HTTP boundaries, command and query buses, application handlers, persistence, messaging, validation, testing and error handling. Controllers translated framework input into commands and queries, which were dispatched to their respective handlers, allowing domain logic to remain independent from the HTTP layer. CQRS, SOLID principles, clean code, carefully selected design patterns and strict automated testing were central to the engineering approach.

I also contributed to the development of the platform’s engineering workflow and runtime infrastructure. This included Docker Compose environments for development, performance and frontend work; PHP workers running on OpenSwoole; Redis Cluster; MySQL; LocalStack; and observability tooling based on Elasticsearch, Kibana and APM. I drove custom tooling for managing development environments, including Alfred for development environment management, and the worker lifecycle tooling built around Foreman for starting, stopping, deploying and monitoring workers across hosts.

The work covered a broad service-oriented platform with bounded contexts including purchasing and payments, warehouse operations, delivery, product information, taxation and scheduled jobs. GitLab CI/CD pipelines were used to test, build and deploy the services, while OpenAPI contracts, shared platform components and common development conventions helped keep the different contexts aligned.

I started as Backend Tech Lead on the Core application team, focused on the design and development of the backend layer for Scalefast’s next-generation e-commerce platform. The application was API-centric and microservices-based, with Domain-Driven Design, CQRS and extensive automated testing as core architectural principles.

The technical stack was based on PHP 8.x, selected parts of the Laravel framework and well-known, battle-tested packages from the League ecosystem. The platform used MySQL and Redis for persistence and infrastructure, Docker-based development environments, and GitLab CI/CD pipelines to test, build and deploy the applications.

A major part of my role was leading the migration from Laravel-based APIs to a custom lightweight framework developed in-house. The new foundation was built on Slim 4, Doctrine and robust PHP components, while following PSR standards and reducing the coupling between the application and the underlying framework.

The application layer established a consistent way of translating PSR HTTP requests into commands and queries, dispatching them through buses to their handlers, and transforming the results back into framework responses. This approach helped keep business logic independent from the transport layer and provided a common structure for the different services and bounded contexts.

I worked across the platform foundation and contributed to the patterns later used by OMS, Fulfillment and other domain contexts. These included purchase and payment flows, warehouse operations, delivery, product information, taxation and scheduled jobs. The work involved defining application boundaries, integrating Doctrine repositories and infrastructure services, supporting asynchronous workers, and maintaining consistent testing and deployment practices across the services.

I also contributed to the Docker-based development workflow and to the GitLab pipelines used for automated testing, application builds and deployments. The role combined hands-on backend development with technical leadership, architectural decision-making and the establishment of reusable conventions for a growing service-oriented PHP platform.

Responsible for the planning, design, architecture and development of the company's new video ad server using PHP and LUA, writing clean code with a focus on high performance and scalability. The technical stack is Openresty (NGINX on steroids), PHP 7.3, Symfony 4.*, MySQL and Redis. The cloud provider is AWS. Elastic Beanstalk for deployment tasks. More details on request.

Responsible for the analysis, definition and development of the API Rest of the Spazious platform using Python, Django and the Django Rest Framework. Responsible for infrastructure and deployment tasks in AWS including Elastic Beanstalk, S3 and Elasticache. More details on request.

Responsible for planning, designing the architecture and developing new features for the company's ad server application, implementing code with a focus on high performance and scalability. The technical stack consists of PHP 5.x, Slim Framework, Memcached, Redis, MongoDB, MySQL and PHPUnit. Extensive use of AWS services and Docker containers to develop the project infrastructure. More details on request.

details.name: Crate
details.description:
Crate is an open-source, self-hosted music platform for managing, analysing, discovering and listening to a personal music library. I designed and built it as a distributed system that combines library ingestion, metadata enrichment, audio analysis, playback, search, discovery and federation between trusted instances.

The platform scans and indexes local music collections, extracts technical and musical metadata, enriches releases and tracks from external sources, and maintains a searchable catalogue. It also processes audio using analysis tools and models to derive features that can be used for similarity, discovery and organisation. The system supports playlists, playback, library exploration, cover art and a progressive web application, with additional support for native clients through Capacitor.

Crate is composed of a FastAPI backend, React-based administration and listening applications, asynchronous Python workers for ingestion and processing, and a Go read plane for efficient catalogue and playback-oriented queries. PostgreSQL is used for persistent data, Redis supports caching and background processing, and the complete system is packaged and operated with Docker and Traefik.

The project includes workflows for file scanning, metadata normalisation, background jobs, audio feature extraction, search, recommendations and synchronisation between services. It is also an exploration of how to design a self-hosted product with clear service boundaries, asynchronous processing and a responsive user experience while keeping deployment accessible to individual users.

details.name: Granite for PHP
details.description:
Granite is a sophisticated zero-dependency PHP library I developed for building immutable, type-safe data transfer objects with advanced validation and auto-mapping capabilities. The library features a comprehensive validation system using PHP 8 attributes, intelligent object-to-object mapping with convention-based property matching (supporting camelCase, snake_case, PascalCase, and custom naming conventions), and robust serialization/deserialization mechanisms for seamless data transformation between different object types and formats (arrays, JSON).

The project demonstrates advanced PHP 8+ features including attributes, enums, readonly classes, and reflection-based metaprogramming. It incorporates enterprise-level patterns such as caching strategies (memory, shared, persistent), profile-based mapping configurations, bidirectional transformations, and a flexible validation rule system that supports both attribute-based and programmatic rule definitions. The architecture emphasizes type safety, immutability, and performance optimization through intelligent caching and lazy evaluation of mapping configurations.

details.name: Sentinel
details.description:
Developed a comprehensive Laravel package for intelligent content moderation and sentiment analysis, supporting multiple AI providers including Google Cloud Language, AWS, TisaneAI, PerspectiveAI, and Azure AI services. The library features a sophisticated local profanity detection engine with 10+ detection strategies including pattern matching, n-gram analysis, phonetic variations, and zero-width character detection. Implemented context-aware analysis capabilities that dynamically adjust moderation thresholds based on content type (educational, medical, social media, etc.) and target audience (children, teens, adults, professional), ensuring appropriate content filtering for different scenarios.

The package incorporates advanced performance optimizations including Laravel Octane support for concurrent processing, intelligent caching mechanisms, and early termination algorithms for efficient large-text analysis. Built with modern PHP 8.3+ features, comprehensive PHPStan level max compliance, and extensive test coverage using Pest 3 framework. The library provides detailed sentiment analysis, confidence scoring, category classification, and maintains multi-language support with configurable detection rules and customizable replacement strategies for flagged content.

details.name: Laravel Devices
details.description: Developed a comprehensive security and session management package for Laravel applications that provides advanced user device tracking, multi-session management with geolocation, and integrated two-factor authentication using Google Authenticator. The package includes features such as device hijacking detection, client-side fingerprinting using FingerprintJS, optimized caching system, custom middleware for automatic tracking, RESTful APIs for device/session management, and a robust event system. The solution is designed as a reusable library with support for multiple data transports (cookies, headers, session), console commands for maintenance tasks, and flexible configuration for different production environments.

manfredSpecificData.goodPractices:
I use Domain-Driven Design when it helps model complex business domains and protect important boundaries. My approach is pragmatic: I focus on clear bounded contexts, explicit domain boundaries, meaningful use cases and keeping business logic independent from frameworks, transports and infrastructure.

I favour simple, readable and maintainable code over clever abstractions. I use SOLID principles, PSR standards, composition, explicit dependencies and well-defined interfaces. I avoid premature generalisation and introduce patterns only when they solve a real problem or protect an important architectural boundary.

I consider automated testing part of the design process, not just a final verification step. I use unit, integration, API and contract tests where they provide value, with special attention to business rules, persistence boundaries, asynchronous workflows and backwards compatibility.

I promote AI-assisted development as a disciplined engineering practice rather than an isolated code-generation activity. AI agents can support discovery, architecture exploration, implementation, testing, review and documentation, provided that the workflow includes clear boundaries, explicit acceptance criteria and automated feedback. I establish the context, conventions and quality gates that allow agents to contribute effectively, while engineers retain ownership of the design, trade-offs and final implementation.

I value automated CI/CD pipelines, reproducible development environments, clear API contracts, useful observability and secure defaults. I pay particular attention to database access patterns, indexing, asynchronous processing, failure handling and tenant isolation when performance, scalability or data boundaries are involved.

Finally, I believe good engineering includes good developer experience. Tools, documentation, conventions and workflows should make the correct path easy to follow while leaving enough flexibility for experienced engineers to make informed decisions.
